title: How to Organise a Group Safari in East Africa, From the First Headcount to the Final Payment
meta_title: How to Organise a Group Safari Without the Headaches
meta_description: How to organise a group safari: dates, routes, vehicles, rooming, split payments and free places, explained by a Nairobi team. Start planning early.
excerpt: How to organise a group safari in East Africa, step by step: headcount, dates, route, vehicles, rooming, deposits and free places for the organiser.
content:
To organise a group safari, fix your headcount, dates and budget first, then choose a country and route that suits the slowest and keenest members alike. Book camps and permits 9 to 12 months ahead, collect deposits, and leave vehicles, transfers and guides to one local operator who handles everything on the ground.

Whether you lead a camera club, a family reunion, a company team or a group of old university friends, the hard part when you organise a group safari is rarely the wildlife. It is the spreadsheets, the payments and keeping twenty opinions happy. This guide walks through each decision in order, and our organise a group safari planning page covers how we take that load off the organiser.

Quick Facts

  • Easiest group size: 6 to 16 travellers, filling one to three safari vehicles
  • Free places: The seventh place is free for every six paying travellers
  • Deposit: 30 to 40% to hold the booking, balance 2 to 4 weeks before travel
  • Payments and flights: Each traveller can pay separately and arrive on a different flight
  • Lead time: 12 months for July to October and Christmas; 6 to 9 months otherwise
  • Gorilla groups: Up to 8 visitors per gorilla family per day in Rwanda and Uganda

What Does It Take to Organise a Group Safari?

It takes five decisions made in the right order: who is coming, when, where, how much, and who will run it. When you organise a group safari in that sequence, each answer narrows the next, and you avoid the classic mistake of falling for a lodge before you know whether twelve people can sleep there.

Most organisers start with a destination and work backwards. That works for two people, but a group needs firmer foundations. A rough headcount tells you how many vehicles and rooms you need. Dates decide park fees, prices and whether the wildebeest are in Kenya or Tanzania. Budget then rules routes and lodges in or out.

Step by step: how to organise a group safari

The timeline below is the one we suggest to anyone who wants to organise a group safari for ten or more people in a busy month. Quieter months and smaller groups can compress it, but the order of the steps stays the same.

WhenWhat the organiser does
12 months outSend a short interest survey: dates that work, budget band, must-see animals, mobility needs
10 to 12 months outAsk a local operator for a draft route and group quote; hold rooms and gorilla permits
9 months outConfirm the headcount, collect 30 to 40% deposits and send the rooming list
4 to 6 months outTravellers book flights; share arrival times, passport details and dietary needs
2 to 4 weeks outBalances paid; final briefing on visas, insurance, health and packing
Arrival weekAirport meet and greet, welcome briefing and vehicle allocation in Nairobi or Arusha

When Should Your Group Travel?

Your group should travel in the dry season of the country you choose, unless price matters more than perfect conditions. In Kenya and Tanzania the main dry months are late June to October, with a shorter dry spell from January to February. Rwanda and Uganda are driest from June to September and December to February.

If you organise a group safari around the dry season, book earliest, because those are also the months when camps fill first.

When you organise a group safari, dates affect the budget more than they would for a couple, because every saving is multiplied by the headcount. The Masai Mara National Reserve charges non-resident adults US$100 a day from January to June and US$200 a day from July to December (checked November 2026). For a group of twelve on three Mara days, that difference alone adds up to thousands of dollars, so always confirm current fees before you collect deposits.

The Great Migration usually reaches the Mara from about July, while the calving herds sit in the southern Serengeti from January to March. Botswana and Namibia are at their best in the dry winter months from May or June to October. School groups and families are tied to holidays, so they often get the best value by choosing green-season months such as November or early December, when parks are quieter and lodges are more flexible with rooms.

Our guide to the best time to visit Kenya breaks the months down further if you are still choosing dates.

Which Country and Route Suits Your Group?

The right country depends on what holds your group together. Kenya suits first-timers and mixed ages, with short drives from Nairobi and a huge choice of lodges. Tanzania adds the Serengeti and Ngorongoro Crater. Uganda and Rwanda are for gorillas, and Botswana and Namibia suit groups who want space, deserts or water safaris.

Think about the group's purpose before you organise a group safari around a map. A camera club wants long days and fewer people per vehicle. A family reunion wants pools, family rooms and midday rests. A company team wants a smooth, impressive programme with a gala dinner. The table below matches common group types to a starting route.

Group typeA route that tends to workWhere to start
Clubs and societiesSamburu, Ol Pejeta, Lake Nakuru and the Masai MaraClub and society safaris
Families and reunionsAmboseli, Lake Naivasha and the Masai MaraFamily and multi-generation safaris
Companies and incentivesMasai Mara by air, or Kigali with gorilla trekkingCorporate and incentive safaris
Schools and universitiesNairobi, Lake Naivasha, Lake Nakuru and a conservancyStudent and study tour safaris
Birthdays, weddings and girls' tripsThe Mara or Serengeti plus a Zanzibar beach finishSpecial occasion group safaris

Two of our ready-made trips show how to organise a group safari in practice. The 6 day Kenya family safari covers Amboseli, Lake Naivasha, Lake Nakuru and the Masai Mara with short drives and a boat ride, while the 7 day Kenya camera club safari runs pop-up Land Cruisers with bean bags and charging points through Samburu, Ol Pejeta and the Mara.

How Many Vehicles, Rooms and Guides Does a Group Need?

A group needs enough vehicles for everyone to have a window seat, enough rooms in one camp for the whole party, and one guide per vehicle. When you organise a group safari, these three numbers are worked out together, because the vehicle plan drives the cost and the camp choice limits the size.

Vehicles and seating

Safari groups in Kenya and Tanzania usually travel in 4x4 Land Cruisers with pop-up roofs, each with its own driver guide. When you organise a group safari, plan seats so nobody is stuck in the middle for a week. Photography groups need even more space for long lenses, which is why our camera club trips carry fewer people per vehicle than a standard safari.

Rooms and rooming lists

Many smaller safari camps have only a dozen or so tents, so a group of 16 may fill one completely. Anyone who wants to organise a group safari in a small camp should send the rooming list early: who shares, who needs a single, which rooms must sit close together for children or older travellers. Single rooms usually carry a supplement, and that should be shown separately so couples are not paying for it.

Permits with daily limits

If you organise a group safari with gorillas in it, permits are where group size matters most. Rwanda and Uganda allow up to eight visitors per gorilla family per day, so a group of fourteen needs permits for two families on the same morning. Our guide to group gorilla trekking in Uganda explains how to split a large party, and Rwanda's permit is USD 1,500 per foreign non-resident (checked November 2026).

Why Does a Group Pay Less Per Head?

A group safari costs less per person than a private safari for two, because vehicle, guide and transfer costs are shared, but park fees and lodge rates stay per head. The bigger the share of fixed costs in your trip, the more you save by filling every seat in every vehicle.

A useful way to read any quote when you organise a group safari is to split it into three parts. Shared costs fall as the group grows. Per-person costs stay the same however many travel. Optional extras let each member choose their own trip without pushing up everyone else's price.

Cost typeExamplesWhat changes with group size
Shared costsSafari vehicles, driver guides, fuel, airport transfersFalls per person as each vehicle fills
Per-person costsPark and conservancy fees, lodge beds, gorilla permits, mealsStays the same per person
Free placesSeventh place free for every six paying travellersLowers the average price or covers the leader
Optional extrasBalloon safaris, spa treatments, Zanzibar extensionPaid only by those who choose them

We quote every group personally, because dates, headcount and room types change the price. Our full Kenya park fees guide shows the per-person fees you can budget for, and those do not drop because you travel together.

Payments, Flights and Paperwork for the Whole Party

Payments, flights and travel documents are where most group trips go wrong, so when you organise a group safari, put clear rules in writing at the start. Decide who pays whom, set deadlines a week before the operator's own deadlines, and keep one shared list of passports, flights and insurance numbers.

Deposits and split payments

On our group bookings, a deposit of 30 to 40% holds the booking and the balance is due 2 to 4 weeks before travel. Each traveller can pay their own share, so the organiser does not have to collect money from twenty people. Cancellation rules are set out in our terms and conditions, and it is worth sharing them with every member before they pay.

Flights from different cities

Group members can arrive on different flights, which matters when you organise a group safari for people coming from London, Houston and Singapore. We match airport transfers to each arrival, and many groups add a first night in Nairobi so late arrivals can rest before the first long drive. Fly-in safaris suit groups short on time, but light aircraft have tight soft-bag limits, so tell everyone early.

Visas, insurance and health

Most visitors to Kenya need an eTA from the official Kenya eTA website, applied for at least three days before travel. Our Kenya eTA guide walks through the form, and groups visiting Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda can look at the East Africa Tourist Visa. Ask every member to buy cover with medical evacuation; our travel insurance page explains what to look for.

Insider Tips for Group Organisers

  • Set a deposit deadline: Treat whoever pays by the date as confirmed and let late payers join a waiting list
  • Name a deputy: Anyone who sets out to organise a group safari needs a second contact in case the organiser falls ill or misses a flight
  • Share one document: Keep passports, flights, diets and insurance in one shared file
  • Plan a slow first day: Long-haul arrivals and a long drive on the same day tire a whole group
  • Mix the vehicles: Rotate seats and vehicle groups so cliques do not form
  • Keep money simple: Quote extras separately so nobody pays for activities they skip

Frequently Asked Questions

How far ahead should we organise a group safari?

Start about 12 months ahead if you want to organise a group safari for July to October or around Christmas, because the best camps and gorilla permits sell out first. Nine months is usually enough for quieter months. Groups of fewer than ten can sometimes plan in four to six months, but the choice of lodges shrinks quickly.

Do group members have to pay together or fly in together?

No. On our group bookings each traveller can pay their own share, and people can arrive on different flights. A deposit of 30 to 40% holds the booking and the balance is due 2 to 4 weeks before travel. The organiser only needs to send names, rooming and flight details so we can match transfers to every arrival.

Does the group organiser travel free?

Often, yes. For every six paying travellers the seventh place on our group safaris is free, so a group of twelve paying travellers earns two free places. Most groups give the free place to the person who organises the group safari, a teacher or a club leader, or they split its value across everyone's price.

What is the ideal size for a group safari?

Groups of six to sixteen are the easiest size to organise a group safari around. Six fills one vehicle and earns a free place, while sixteen still fits most mid-size camps and two gorilla families in Rwanda or Uganda. Larger groups work well too, but they need more vehicles, more rooms in one camp and earlier booking.

Is a private group safari better than joining a scheduled tour?

For most friends, families, clubs and teams, yes. A private group safari runs on your dates, your pace and your route, and nobody shares your vehicle with strangers. A scheduled tour can be cheaper for one or two people, but once you have six travellers the private group usually costs about the same per person and gives far more control.

Final Thoughts

The organisers who enjoy their own trip are the ones who organise a group safari in the right order: they settle numbers, dates and money rules early, then let someone else carry the logistics.
